hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? on a rough day, when someone asks how you are, what do you usually say?
options: most of us do. today, a word that’s more honest than fine.
good. today’s word sits right next to the truth.
fair. today’s word works for anyone who asks.

steps.line: One day, two men were sitting near the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. Then both of them sneezed.

steps.q: He blesses one of them, and not the other. Why do you think?
o: Only one of them said alhamdulillah
steps.why: Only one praised God. The report is in Bukhari: the Prophet ﷺ answered the praise, not the sneeze.

steps.line: To one he said, “Yarhamuk Allah,” may God have mercy on you. To the other, nothing. The other man asked him why.
“This one praised God,” he said, “and you didn’t.” The first man had said “alhamdulillah”: the praise belongs to God.
Another saying made it a habit: sneeze, say alhamdulillah, and whoever hears you answers, “yarhamuk Allah.” Muslims still do it, at work and at home.
steps.label: today

steps.line: Hamd, praise, isn’t quite shukr, thanks. Thanks answers a good thing done for you. Praise answers who someone is, on any kind of day.

steps.q: Muslims say alhamdulillah many times in prayer alone. Where does that line come from?
o: A prayer of the prophet Abraham
steps.why: Al-Fatiha, recited in every unit of every prayer, begins “al-hamdu lillah, Lord of the worlds” (1:2). That’s at least seventeen times a day in the five daily prayers.

steps.line: The Prophet ﷺ said the believer’s life is a wonder. When good comes, they’re grateful. When hardship comes, they’re patient. Both are good for them.

steps.q: The Arabic word for patience, sabr, is also the name of a plant. Which one?
steps.why: Sabr also names aloe: bitter to taste, used to heal. Some teachers love the link: patience tastes bitter and does you good.

steps.line: Today, ask a grandmother about her terrible knees, and you may hear it first: alhamdulillah. Not pretending. Praise, whatever the day did.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Many Muslims count alhamdulillah on beads after each prayer. How many times?
steps.why: Thirty-three each of subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar, as in a hadith in Muslim. That’s why many strings have 33 or 99 beads.

say: here’s what i love. the blessing went to the one who praised. a two-second word, and it changed the whole moment.
in islam, alhamdulillah doesn’t pretend the bad day was good. it says the praise belongs to God, whatever the day did. many count it on beads after every prayer.

steps.q: The name Muhammad comes from h-m-d, the same root as hamd. From this lesson, what do you think it means?
steps.why: The praised one, again and again. Ahmad, Mahmoud and Hamid carry the same three letters.

today.say: today, say “alhamdulillah,” or “praise be to God,” once on purpose for something good, and once for something hard. or, if you’d rather, just name both and let them belong to the same day.
options: lovely. the hard one is the brave one.
that’s a good start. the word grows with use.

tomorrow.title: A drink for a thirsty dog.
tomorrow.line: a man, a deep well, a dog panting in the heat. and the Lord of every world.

sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 6221 and 6225; Sahih Muslim 2991 (Anas: two men sneezed near the Prophet; he said “yarhamuk Allah” to one and not the other; “This one praised Allah and that one did not”)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6224 (when one of you sneezes, say al-hamdu lillah; the one who hears says yarhamuk Allah)
Sahih Muslim 2999 (Suhayb: the affair of the believer is a wonder; grateful in good, patient in hardship, both good for him)
Hamd and shukr: the common distinction in tafsir on Qur’an 1:2 (e.g. Ibn Kathir)
Sunan Ibn Majah 3803 (‘A’isha: when he saw something he disliked, he said “al-hamdu lillahi ‘ala kulli hal”)
Sahih Muslim 597 (saying subhanallah, alhamdulillah and Allahu akbar thirty-three times after each prayer)
check: The hamd/shukr line (“thanks answers a good thing done; praise answers who someone is”) is a simplification of the scholarly distinction. Confirm.
Ibn Majah 3803 is graded hasan by some and weak by others; it is used only in a “why” line. Confirm.
